newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Violence flares over land dispute in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Violence flares over land dispute in Vietnam.

text.p: Vietnamese villagers repelled an attempt to appropriate land for a golf course on Tuesday, attacking and burning a truck sent to fence off the land in the second straight day of violence on Hanoi's northern outskirts.

The run-in followed a clash on Monday in which some 600 police officers, many carrying riot shields and wielding electric prods, fought a pitched battle with protesters on a dirt track in Kim No commune, near the Vietnamese capital's airport, according to local residents.
The protesters, estimated to number 500, had hurled stones at police and set two bulldozers and another vehicle on fire.
It was not clear how many were hurt in Monday's violence, though one resident said he saw at least five injured people being taken away.

A Reuters correspondent watched on Tuesday as about 60 people from the commune's hamlet of Tho Da surrounded a truck, one of three sent to fence off the land, on the same dirt track. They hauled its driver and passenger out and set the vehicle alight.

The two accompanying trucks turned around and sped back along the road as smoke billowed from the first. The villagers later threw fencing wire from the burnt-out truck into a pond and remained at the scene until nightfall. An official of the Kim No People's Committee said authorities were still trying to persuade people to give up their land but denied that any violence had occurred.
Riots and demonstrations are rare in communist Vietnam and almost never reported by the state-controlled media.

However, this was not the first incident of unrest at Kim No commune. One woman was killed and scores were injured there last May in violence which erupted when police began ripping up rice plants from a field being appropriated for the golf course.
Three men and one woman were sentenced last month to prison terms of between three and five years for their involvement in that incident.
The planned golf course is part of a $177 million joint-venture project involving South Korea's Daewoo Group, the biggest single foreign investor in Vietnam.
A senior official from the venture, which is called Daeha, declined to comment on the land dispute.

The official Hanoi Moi daily said Kim No's villagers had agreed to vacate the 128-hectare (316-acre) area of land and ponds by December 30 after accepting an offer of a 10-year compensation package worth 20.63 billion dong ($1.85 million).

It said 400 villagers would be hired to work at the golf course when it opens, probably in 1998, and investors would spend thousands of dollars on infrastructure and English-language training in Kim No.

Tran Anh, a resident of a neighbouring village, said the protesters had agreed to the compensation. However, he said they were now demanding the release of the four people jailed for their part in the bloody clash in May.
